title: The units of a calibration residual
lede: Every model is fitted by least squares on per-quote residuals. Dividing each price error by the quote's vega makes every residual read in vol units, at every strike.
eq_labels: 1 · Residual: model price error over vega, floored
2 · What it reads: the vol miss, plus a vomma term far from the fit
3 · Objective (mid target; bands on the next slide)
paras: Price-space models
LQD and local volatility produce $c_\theta$ as a price, which keeps every iterate a valid density; the division by vega moves the error to vol units.
Vol-space models
SVI and MCS produce $\sigma_\theta$ directly: their residual is exactly $\Delta\sigma_i$.
The floor $\eta$
where vega is tiny — far wings, last days — the residual stops amplifying and behaves like a scaled price error.

head: Symbol
Meaning
rows: Market implied vol and total variance $w_i = \sigma_i^2\tau$
Black call price in forward units: price $/\,(DF)$
Model call price in the same units, and its implied vol
Black vega at the market vol, $\varphi(d_+)\sqrt{\tau}$; fixed per quote during the fit
Quote weight: one vote per quote by default

example: A 0.04 USD price error on an option with a vega of 20 USD per unit of volatility (0.20 USD per vol point): $r = 0.04/20 = 0.002$, that is 20 vol bp. The currency cancels. Far from the fit the vomma term appears: a 100 vol bp miss at $k = 0.2$ ($\sigma = 25\%$, $\tau = 0.25$) reads as 105 vol bp; at the money it reads as 100.
notes: Every model in the app is fitted the same way. There is one residual per quote. The residuals are squared, weighted and summed, and the model's own penalty rows are added on top. This slide is about the unit of one residual.

The first line is the residual. The density models, LQD and local volatility, produce prices. The numerator is the model's call price at the quote's log-moneyness, minus Black's price of the market quote. Both are in forward units: the price divided by the discount factor and the forward. That difference is a price error. It is divided by the Black vega at the market vol, plus a small floor.

Why divide? Least squares assumes the noise has the same size everywhere, in the units of the residual. In price units, a miss of 50 vol basis points is worth about ten times less in the wings than at the money. A price fit would all but ignore the wings. After the division, every residual reads in vol units at every strike.

The second line says how exact that is. Expand the price in the vol. The first term is vega times the vol miss, so the residual is the vol miss. The next term is a vomma correction: the product of Black's two d terms, divided by the vol, times half the miss. At the money it vanishes. In the wing it grows. A miss of 100 vol bp at a log-moneyness of 0.2, with 25 percent vol and three months to expiry, reads as 105. Near the optimum the misses are small and the residual is the vol error. Early in a cold fit that is only approximately true.
SVI and MCS produce vols directly, so their residual is exactly the vol miss. The result is one unit for every model. An RMS of 20 bp means the same thing on all four.

The floor. Where vega is tiny, several standard deviations out or in the last days of an expiry, a small price error would become a huge vol error. The floor stops that. Below the floor the residual behaves like a scaled price error, which is all the information such a quote carries.

The strip is the same arithmetic in dollars. A four-cent price error on an option with 20 dollars of vega per unit of volatility, that is 20 cents per vol point, gives 0.002. That is 20 vol bp. The currency cancels.

The third line is the objective: the sum of the weighted squared residuals, plus the model's penalties. Two choices are left, and they are the next two slides. What target inside the bid-ask the residual is measured from, and how much each quote weighs.
Transition: next, the mid in the first line is replaced by a band: mid, bid-ask or haircut targets.

If asked why LQD is not fitted on implied vols directly: the model works in price space, and that is what keeps every iterate a valid density. Dividing by vega gives vol units without inverting the model's price at every step.
If asked whose vega is in the denominator: the market's. It is the Black vega at the quote's own vol, so it stays fixed while the parameters move.

title: Mid, bid–ask and haircut targets
lede: A band target allows a range of fitted values, with a weak mid anchor selecting among them.
paras: Mid
Minimise the squared difference to the quoted mid.
Band
Penalise values outside the interval. Inside it, only the mid-anchor term remains.
Haircut
Move each side toward mid by $h$, stopping at mid. A spread narrower than $2h$ collapses to a mid target.
alt: Illustrative loss curves comparing a mid target with a band and a trimmed band
caption: Illustrative 19% / 21% quote. A 0.5 vol-point haircut leaves [19.5%, 20.5%]. The band includes a 0.05 mid-anchor weight.
reference: Note 07 · tolerance and selection within a band
notes: The residual on the previous slide measured the model against one number, the mid. But the market quotes an interval, bid to ask. Any value inside it is consistent with the quote. This slide shows the three targets the app offers.

The formula, per quote. The model's value at the quote, the lower and upper edges of the target band, and the mid. All of them are in the residual units of the previous slide, so in vol. The first two terms are zero inside the band and grow quadratically outside it. The third is a weak pull toward the mid. Its weight, theta mid on the slide, is 0.05 by default.
Mid mode is the plain parabola, the grey curve. Every quote is treated as known exactly at its mid. It is the default.

Bid-ask mode is the blue curve: nearly flat inside the spread, quadratic outside. Why keep the weak anchor at all? With the bands alone, a whole family of curves has zero cost. On a clean chain that flat valley measured 126 vol basis points wide, and the solver would stop wherever it first entered it. The anchor picks one answer: of all the curves the bands accept, the one closest to the mids.

Haircut mode, the orange curve, trims each side toward the mid by the haircut, half a vol point by default, and never past the mid. A spread narrower than twice the haircut collapses to a mid target. So tight at-the-money quotes behave as mids, while wide wing quotes keep a real tolerance. On the slide's 19 to 21 percent quote, a half-point haircut leaves 19.5 to 20.5.

Worked through: a model at 20.4 percent sits inside both intervals and pays only the anchor. A model at 20.8 is inside the raw band but 0.3 vol point above the trimmed one, so the haircut target charges it.

What a band buys. Inside the band the data term is twenty times weaker, so the model's own regularisation wins there. On a rigid model, mid and band fits stay close: 6 vol bp apart in the reference example. On a flexible model with a smoothness penalty they separate by 47 vol bp. The mid fit follows the tick bounce; the band fit cuts through it. With no smoothness penalty at all the band gains nothing, because the anchor points back at the mids.

Reading the RMS. It measures the objective actually minimised. In bid-ask mode that is the distance outside the band. So a fit sitting inside every band reports close to zero even when it is far from the mids. Compare models only under the same target.
One link back to quote synchronisation: in band and haircut modes, a stale quote's band is widened by its age allowance on each side.
Transition: the target says what each residual is measured against. Next: how much each quote counts, the weights.

If asked which target to use: mid is the default and suits a tight, clean chain. Bid-ask or haircut pay off on wide or noisy quotes with a flexible model, where they let the smoothness penalty do its job. The haircut moves continuously between the two.

If asked whether the band is a hard constraint: no, a soft one. Outside the band the cost grows quadratically, so a strong pull elsewhere can still push the fit past an edge. It does so by about a twentieth of what the same pull would do in mid mode.
demo: Show the target shading on the Smile, then the Mid / Bid–Ask / Haircut controls in Calibration options.

title: Quote weights and strike spacing
lede: The weights decide which parts of the smile the fit cares about: the exchange's listing (equal weights), or a chosen target.
eq_labels: 1 · Target schemes: target shape × spacing, capped, mean one
2 · Spacing: width of the quote's Voronoi cell
3 · Equal weighting, the default: one vote per quote
paras: Target $f$
the shape the summed weight should follow along the smile: flat, option time value, vega or OTM delta.
Voronoi cell
the stretch of log-moneyness closer to this quote than to any other; its width $s_i$ is half the gap to each neighbour, so dense clusters get narrow cells.
Equal weighting
every quote counts once, with no spacing correction. The summed weight then follows the exchange's listing — heaviest where strikes are densest, usually near the money.
alt: Reference figure of quote weights across strikes under equal and time-value-density weighting
caption: Reference-note chain: grey, equal weights, 1 per quote; green, the time-value target with the spacing correction. Isolated strikes gain weight, clustered ones share it, and the target fades the far wings.
example: Near the money, three quotes 0.01 apart; in the wing, one quote alone in a stretch of 0.03. Equal weights give the cluster 3 votes to 1. With the flat target, each clustered quote stands for 0.01 and the lone quote for 0.03, so both stretches of the smile weigh the same.
notes: The first line: every scheme except equal is a target times a spacing correction. The target is the shape the summed weight should follow along the smile: flat, time value, vega or OTM delta. The spacing is the width of the quote's Voronoi cell, the stretch of log-moneyness closer to that quote than to any other. In one dimension that is simply half the gap to the left neighbour plus half the gap to the right. That is the second line. The two end quotes take their one gap.

Why the spacing? Think of the objective as an integral of squared error along the smile, weighted by the target. On an irregular grid, the sum that approximates it multiplies each quote by the width it stands for. Without that width, listing more strikes in one area would change the objective even though the smile had not moved.

Two safeguards. The spacing multiplier is capped at ten times the average cell, so an isolated far-wing quote cannot dominate. And the weights are rescaled to mean one, so switching scheme does not change the balance between the data and the regularisation.

Equal weighting, the third line, is the default and the odd one out: one vote per quote, no correction. The fit then emphasises wherever the exchange lists the most strikes, usually near the money. That emphasis is set by the listing, not by any choice in the app. Only on a grid evenly spaced in log-strike does it coincide with the flat target. The figure compares it, in grey, with the time-value target in green.

The strip makes it concrete. Near the money, three quotes a hundredth apart. In the wing, one quote alone in a stretch of 0.03. Equal weights give the cluster three votes to one. With the flat target and the spacing correction, each clustered quote stands for 0.01 and the lone quote for 0.03, so both stretches of the smile weigh the same.
Weights are independent of the target on the previous slide. The fit mode chooses what each residual is measured against; the scheme chooses how much each residual counts.
Transition: with residuals, targets and weights defined, the next slide turns to the models themselves, and what each one parameterises.

If asked which scheme to use: equal is the default. The flat target makes every stretch of the smile count the same when strikes are unevenly listed. Vega, delta and time value fade the wings at increasing speed. Vega keeps the most wing weight, time value the least.
demo: Smile view: switch the Weights layer on in the layer rail — the strip under the chart shows the target beside the weight the fit sums; hover a bar for k · target · ×spacing · weight.

title: What each model parameterises
lede: The four families place flexibility in different mathematical objects.

head: Model
Unknown object
Pricing / inversion
Main constraints or controls
rows: Wing budget; positivity and density checks

example: Use the same prepared quotes, forward, variance clock, target mode and weighting. Record the tail and regularisation choices alongside the fit error.
notes: Four models. What separates them is not the number of parameters. It is the mathematical object each one describes.

LQD describes a probability law, through the log of its quantile slope. It prices by integrating that law, so every fit is arbitrage-free by construction. The only condition is a finite forward: the right tail scale below one, as the next slide shows.

SVI in jump-wing coordinates describes total implied variance as a function of log-moneyness. It is a tilted hyperbola, read through five desk handles: ATM variance, ATM skew, the two wing slopes and the minimum variance. It prices through Black. Its wings are bounded by construction. But an SVI slice that passes the usual screens can still carry a negative density, so the app checks the density of every displayed slice explicitly.

MCS, the multi-core sigmoid, adds detail in the body. A convex base sets the wings and the overall skew. Up to two signed corrections, humps or notches, are built to vanish in both tails. That is how it fits a W-shaped smile ahead of an event without moving the wing slopes.

Local volatility describes the instantaneous diffusion coefficient: a local variance as a function of time and normalised strike, continuous and piecewise affine on a grid. It prices every quote by marching the forward Dupire equation through all expiries at once. So it is fitted per underlying, not per expiry. Its controls are positive grid values, a roughness penalty, and checks on the pricing lattice.

Two consequences. The regularisers are not interchangeable. An LQD spectral penalty, an MCS correction penalty and an LV roughness penalty act on different objects, even though each is one coefficient in the options. And LQD is the backbone of the app. The prior, the temporal filter and the graph all work on its handles, even when another model is on screen.

The strip is the rule for a fair comparison: the same prepared quotes, forward, variance clock, target and weights. The tail and regularisation settings are recorded next to the error. Even then, an in-sample RMS says nothing about the curve between or beyond the quotes. Compare densities, tails, and behaviour on held-out strikes.
Transition: the next slides open each family, starting with how LQD builds its law.

If asked why keep four models: they fail differently. SVI is rigid and fast but cannot turn twice. MCS adds body detail with fixed wings. LQD guarantees a valid law at every iterate. Local volatility ties all the expiries of an underlying together. Side by side on the same quotes, their differences show the model risk.

If asked which one the app relies on: LQD, the backbone that feeds the prior, the filter and the graph. SVI and MCS are comparators on the same prepared quotes. Local volatility has its own lens and fits the whole ladder.

title: LQD: constructing a probability law
lede: LQD models the distribution of the log-return through the slope of its quantile. Any real function $g$ gives a valid law: one shift and one inequality do the rest.
eq_labels: 1 · Quantile slope: positive for every $g$, so the density is too
2 · The smooth part $g$: endpoint terms and a Legendre body
3 · One shift makes the forward the mean
4 · Tail scales: the quantile's slope in log-odds at each end
paras: Why $A_R < 1$
the forward is the mean $\mathbb{E}[e^{X}]$. In the right tail the density falls like $e^{-x/A_R}$, so $e^{x}e^{-x/A_R}$ is integrable only if $A_R < 1$. The left tail needs no condition.
In the fit
the solver moves $\log A_L$, $\rho$ with $A_R = 1/(1+e^{-\rho})$, and body modes that leave both tails fixed, so every point it visits is an admissible law.

head: Symbol
Meaning
rows: Log-return to expiry: terminal spot over the forward
Rank in $(0,1)$ and the quantile: $\mathbb{P}(X \le Q(u)) = u$
Quantile slope, and the density of $X$: at matching ranks $f_X = 1/q$
Any real function: the model's parameters live here
Endpoint terms of $g$; alone they are not the tail scales
Body coefficients on Legendre polynomials, $n = 2 \ldots N$; $N = 16$ by default
Left and right tail scales: $A_L = e^{L+\sum_n a_n}$, $A_R = e^{R+\sum_n (-1)^n a_n}$

example: All $a_n = 0$ and $L = R = \log s$: then $g \equiv \log s$ and $X = \mu + s\log\frac{U}{1-U}$ with $U$ uniform, a logistic law with $A_L = A_R = s$. An SPX-like fit has $A_L = 0.157$, $A_R = 0.038$: each further 0.157 of log-return down divides the probability by $e$, each 0.038 up does the same. The heavier left tail is the skew.
notes: LQD does not model the smile. It models the distribution, through its quantile. The variable is the log-return to expiry: the log of terminal spot over the forward. Its quantile at rank u is the level the log-return stays below with probability u. The rank runs from zero to one.

The first line: the model is the slope of the quantile. That slope is a fixed skeleton, one over the product of the rank and one minus the rank, multiplied by the exponential of a smooth function g. Because of the exponential, the slope is positive whatever g is. So the quantile increases, and the density, which at each rank is one over that slope, is positive. That is the whole no-arbitrage mechanism. No constraint and no penalty, for any parameters.

The second line: g is the model. It has two endpoint terms, L and R on the slide, and a Legendre expansion for the body. The body runs from the second mode up to the order N, sixteen by default. The low modes read like desk quantities. The second mode bends the smile symmetrically: the butterfly. The third tilts it: the risk reversal. The fourth works the shoulders.

The third line: integrating the slope gives the quantile up to a constant, the shift. The shift is set so that the mean of terminal spot over forward is one, which says the forward is the expected terminal spot. Shifting the log-return by a constant multiplies that mean by the exponential of the constant, so one scalar solves the condition exactly.

The fourth line, the tails. Near the ends, the quantile grows like the log-odds of the rank, and its slope there is the exponential of g at that end. Those two slopes are the left and right tail scales. In return space they are exponential tails. In the left tail, each further step down of one left tail scale divides the probability by e. In the right tail, each further step up of one right tail scale does the same.

Why the right tail scale must be below one. The forward is the mean of terminal spot over forward. In the right tail the density falls like an exponential with rate one over the right tail scale. Multiplied by the exponential of the return, that is integrable only if the right tail scale is below one. At one or above, the forward would be infinite. The left tail needs nothing, because the exponential of the return vanishes there. This is the only condition on the whole parameter space. And the fit removes even that: it moves a free coordinate, rho on the slide, and the right tail scale is the logistic of rho. So every point the fit visits is admissible.

One caution on reading the endpoint terms. Every body mode also moves g at the endpoints, so L and R alone are not the tail scales. The exact relation is in the table. That is why the fit uses the tail scales themselves as coordinates, with body modes that vanish at both ends.

The strip. Switch off the body and set the two endpoint terms equal, to the log of a scale s. Then g is constant, the quantile is linear in the log-odds, and the log-return is a logistic variable with both tail scales equal to s. A real SPX-like fit gives a left tail scale of 0.157 and a right tail scale of 0.038. A much heavier left tail than right: that is the skew.
Transition: next, from this quantile to option prices, in one integral.

If asked how the tail scales relate to Lee's wing slopes: directly. The last finite moment is one over the right tail scale minus one on the right, and one over the left tail scale on the left. Lee's formula maps those to the asymptotic slopes of total variance. For the SPX-like fit the slopes are 0.019 and 0.073, far below Lee's ceiling of 2.

If asked about the generalised tails: these formulas are the exponential-tail case, tail exponent zero. The generalised family adds a per-underlier tail exponent, fixed outside the optimiser. Exponent zero reproduces this slide exactly.
demo: Parametric ▸ Density ▸ Log Q-density: the two logarithmic walls at the ends and the Legendre body between them; Density and CDF are one click away.

title: LQD: from the quantile to option prices
lede: A call is exercised on every rank above its strike's rank. Its price is the stock those outcomes deliver minus the strike they pay: two running sums along the quantile.
eq_title: Strike rank $u_k$: $Q(u_k) = k$, so $\mathbb{P}(X \le k) = u_k$
eq_labels: 1 · The payoff, rank by rank: exercised on the ranks above $u_k$
2 · Split: asset share minus strike cash
3 · The asset share: the stock delivered above rank $u$
4 · If $X$ is normal with variance $w$: the two legs are Black's
paras: Asset share $G(u)$
the part of the forward's value delivered by the outcomes above rank $u$. It falls from 1 at $u = 0$ to 0 at $u = 1$: an asset-or-nothing digital, in forward units.
Strike cash

on exercise the holder pays the strike, $e^{k} = K/F$ per unit of forward, in the fraction $1-u_k$ of outcomes: the strike times a cash-or-nothing digital. The price is what is received minus what is paid.
Every strike from one build
$Q$ and $G$ are computed once per parameter set; each strike then costs one root, $Q(u_k) = k$, and two look-ups.

head: Symbol
Meaning
rows: Call price in forward units, $C/(DF)$, at $k = \log(K/F)$
Log-return $\log(S_T/F_T)$ and its quantile at rank $u$
The strike's rank: outcomes below it expire worthless
Probability that the call finishes in the money
Asset share: the forward's value delivered above rank $u$

example: Logistic law, $A_L = A_R = 0.0813$: ATM vol exactly 20% at $\tau = 0.5$. Strike 110.52 on a forward of 100 ($k = 0.10$): rank $u_k = 0.7965$, so exercised in 20.35% of outcomes. Asset share 24.72, strike cash $110.52 \times 0.2035 = 22.49$: price 2.23, implied vol 20.60%.
notes: The previous slide built the law of the log-return. This one prices an option with it, and the whole calculation fits in one line.

The first line. A call pays terminal spot minus strike when it finishes above the strike. In forward units, that is terminal spot over forward minus strike over forward, whenever the log-return is above the strike's log-moneyness. Write the expectation rank by rank. The rank is uniform between zero and one, and the outcome at each rank is the quantile there. The call is exercised exactly on the ranks above the strike's own rank, the rank where the quantile equals the strike's log-moneyness. So the price is the integral, from the strike's rank up to one, of the outcome minus the strike.

The second line splits that integral in two. The first piece is the asset share, read at the strike's rank. The second is the strike cash: the strike in forward units, times the probability of exercise, one minus the strike's rank. The price is the first minus the second.

The third line says what the asset share is. It adds up terminal spot over forward across the ranks above a given rank. So it is the part of the forward's value delivered by the outcomes above that rank: the value of receiving the stock in those outcomes only. At rank zero that is every outcome, and the share is one, because the forward is the mean. At rank one it is none, and the share is zero. On a desk this is an asset-or-nothing digital.

The strike cash. When the call is exercised, the holder pays the strike, which in forward units is the strike over the forward. It is paid in a fraction of outcomes equal to one minus the strike's rank. So its value is the strike times that probability: a cash-or-nothing digital times the strike. Subtracting the strike cash from the asset share means exactly this: what the call receives on exercise, minus what it pays on exercise.

The fourth line ties this to Black-Scholes. If the log-return is normal, the asset share at the strike's rank is Black's first leg, the asset-or-nothing term. The exercise probability is Black's second leg, the cash-or-nothing term. LQD keeps exactly the same two legs, for any law.

Why it is fast. The quantile and the asset share are running sums, built once per parameter set. Every strike then needs one root, the rank where the quantile equals its log-moneyness, and two look-ups. The next slide shows the build.

The worked example. Switch the body off and keep g constant: the logistic law, both tail scales 0.0813, solved so that the ATM vol is exactly 20 percent at six months. Take a strike 10.5 percent above a forward of 100, a log-moneyness of 0.10. Its rank is 0.7965, so the call is exercised in 20.35 percent of outcomes. The stock those outcomes deliver is worth 24.72. The strike, 110.52, paid 20.35 percent of the time, is worth 22.49. The price is the difference, 2.23. That is an implied vol of 20.60 percent, six-tenths of a point above the money. Even this symmetric law has a smile, because its exponential tails are heavier than the lognormal's.
Transition: the fit needs these prices, and their derivatives in every parameter, many times per second. Next: how one build of the slice gives both.

If asked why the exercise probability is not Black's second leg at the implied vol: Black at 20.60 percent says 22.4 percent; the law says 20.35 percent. Black's second leg ignores the slope of the smile. The true probability is minus the strike derivative of the price, and that derivative carries a vega-times-smile-slope term. The two legs differ from Black's one by one; their difference, the price, is the same.

If asked about the closed form behind the example: for a constant g the shift is exact. It is minus the log of pi s over the sine of pi s, which is minus 0.01088 here. The asset share is the upper tail of a beta law with parameters one plus s and one minus s: 0.24722 both ways. The forward's own rank is 53.3 percent. More than half the outcomes end below the forward, because the mean of terminal spot over forward is held at one.
demo: Parametric ▸ Density ▸ CDF: hover at $x = k$ to read the strike's rank $u_k$; one minus it is the chance that the call is exercised.

title: LQD calibration: one build per step, exact derivatives
lede: At each step the solver needs every quote's price and its derivative in every parameter. Both come from one build of the slice: running sums on a fixed grid, read at each strike. The strike's rank moves with the parameters, but that move adds nothing.
eq_title: Parameters $\theta = (L, R, a_2, \ldots, a_N)$; basis $\varphi_j = \partial g/\partial\theta_j$
eq_labels: 1 · A price's derivative: the moving lower limit contributes nothing
2 · The quantile's derivative: one more running sum per parameter
3 · The shift's derivative: the forward stays the mean
eq_note: $\varphi_j$ is $1-u$ for $L$, $u$ for $R$ and $P_n(1-2u)$ for $a_n$: fixed functions, because $g$ is linear in $\theta$, so $\partial q/\partial\theta_j = q\,\varphi_j$. Line 3 differentiates $\int_0^1 e^{Q(u)}\,du = 1$. Line 1 is $\partial G/\partial\theta_j$ read at the fixed rank $u_k$.
paras: Why it matters
finite differences rebuild the slice once more per parameter and re-solve every strike's rank; the exact derivatives reuse the one build, with two more running sums per parameter.
Capacity
the order is cut to two quotes per parameter, $N + 1 \le n/2$ for $n$ quotes, never below 6 (24 quotes: $N = 11$); a ridge $10^{-6}\,n^{2}a_n^{2}$ on the modes $n \ge 4$ damps oscillation.

head: Stage
What the code does
rows: Logistic law: $a_n = 0$, $L = R = \log s$, $s = \sqrt{3w_0}/\pi$ from the quotes' ATM variance $w_0$; in a surface sweep, the previous expiry's fit
2,001 nodes even in log-odds $\log\frac{u}{1-u}$, from $-40$ to 40, where the quantile's slope is $e^{g}$: running sums give $Q$, then $\mu$, then $G$
Newton on the interpolated $Q$ for the rank $u_k$, then $G(u_k) - e^{k}(1-u_k)$
Lines 1–3 for all $N+1$ parameters, on the same grid, read at the same ranks
Trust-region least squares on the quote residuals, the ridge and the $A_R$ barrier; stops at relative changes of $10^{-10}$
One rebuild on 8,001 nodes for the prices, the density and the variance swap

example: SPY 16 October expiry, 121 quotes (23 September): the default order-16 fit takes 26 ms, 14 evaluations, 2.06 vol bp RMS. On a 24-quote synthetic strip today ($N = 11$): 9 ms with the exact derivatives, 23 ms with finite differences, same optimum; the two Jacobians agree to $4 \times 10^{-5}$.
reference: Note 01 · §10 the derivative that comes free; prep Q&A §3
notes: Calibration is the least-squares problem from the residual slide earlier in this section. One vega-scaled price residual per quote, plus a small ridge and the barrier on the right tail scale. A trust-region solver needs two things at every trial parameter vector. The residuals, meaning every quote's model price. And the Jacobian, the derivative of each price in each parameter. This slide is how LQD gets both from one build.

The build. The smooth part g is linear in the parameters, so on a fixed grid it is one matrix product. The grid is even in log-odds, the log of the rank over one minus the rank, from minus 40 to 40. In that coordinate the quantile's slope is simply the exponential of g, and the singular ends of the rank interval are gone. Three running sums follow. Integrate the exponential of g for the quantile. One integral for the shift that makes the mean of terminal spot over forward one. Integrate terminal spot over forward from the right for the asset share. During the fit the grid has 2,001 nodes.
Pricing a quote: find its rank by Newton on the interpolated quantile. A linear seed and four steps reach machine precision. Then asset share minus strike cash, as on the previous slide.

The first line: the derivative of a price. The price is an integral whose lower limit, the strike's rank, moves when the parameters move. Leibniz's rule gives two terms: the integral of the derivative of the integrand, and the integrand at the limit times the speed of the limit. At the limit, the integrand is the payoff at the exercise boundary: the outcome at the strike's rank minus the strike. That is zero by definition of that rank. So the second term drops. There is no need to differentiate the root. It is the same reason the exercise boundary drops out of American option Greeks.

The second line: what remains is the derivative of the quantile. Because g is linear in the parameters, the derivative of the quantile's slope in one parameter is the slope times a fixed basis function. That function is one minus the rank for the left endpoint term, the rank for the right one, and the Legendre polynomial for a body mode. So the derivative of the unshifted quantile is one more running sum, of the slope times the basis function, on the same grid.

The third line: the shift. The mean of terminal spot over forward stays one for every parameter vector. Differentiate that. The change in the shift must cancel the average change of the unshifted quantile, weighted by terminal spot over forward. One integral per parameter.

Put together, the derivative of each price is the derivative of the asset share, read at the quote's rank. That is two extra running sums per parameter on the grid already built. Finite differences would rebuild the slice once more per parameter and re-solve every strike's rank.

Around the solve. The start is the logistic law of the previous slide's example, scaled to the quotes' ATM variance. In a surface sweep each expiry starts from the previous expiry's fit when the orders match. Capacity: the order is capped at two quotes per parameter, never below six. Twenty-four quotes give order 11; 34 quotes or more keep the default 16. The ridge is ten to the minus six times the mode number squared times the mode's coefficient squared, applied from the fourth mode up. That leaves the two lowest body modes free. The accepted fit is rebuilt once on 8,001 nodes for everything displayed.

The strip. Real SPY, the 16 October expiry, 121 quotes, measured on 23 September: the default order-16 fit takes 26 milliseconds, 14 evaluations, an RMS of 2.06 vol basis points. Today, on a 24-quote synthetic strip: 9 milliseconds with the exact derivatives, 23 with finite differences, the same optimum. The two Jacobians agree to four parts in a hundred thousand.
Transition: the same law gives exact ATM handles. Next: the two ways a smile is summarised in three numbers, and which part of the app uses which.

If asked when the exact Jacobian is not used: when an active saved prior adds strike anchors or operator rows, the whole fit falls back to finite differences. Same answer, slower. A variance-swap target on its own keeps the exact path.

If asked about the solver's coordinates: three kinds. The log of the left tail scale, a logistic coordinate for the right tail scale, and body modes that vanish at both ends. That is the chart described on the LQD law slide. It multiplies the Jacobian by the chart's derivative. The optimum does not depend on the chart.

title: Two ways to summarise a smile: ATM handles and delta packages
lede: Three derivatives at the money, or three option packages at fixed deltas. They agree to first order but are different coordinates: the filter and the graph carry the first, the prior's default persists the second.
eq_title: Implied vol $\sigma(k)$ of one expiry; delta-$d$ legs $k_c$ (call) and $k_p$ (put)
eq_labels: 1 · ATM handles: level, skew, curvature — exact on LQD
2 · Delta packages: risk reversal and butterfly
3 · The link: a Taylor expansion at the money, exact only for a quadratic smile
eq_note: $k_c$ solves $k = \tfrac12\sigma(k)^2\tau - \sigma(k)\sqrt{\tau}\,\Phi^{-1}(d)$: the strike whose forward Black call delta is $d$ ($d = 0.25$ for $25\Delta$); $k_p$ uses $1-d$. The legs sit near $\pm 0.67\,\sigma\sqrt{\tau}$ at $25\Delta$ and $\pm 1.28\,\sigma\sqrt{\tau}$ at $10\Delta$. Units: $s_0$ in vol per unit of $k$, $\kappa_0$ per unit of $k^2$; RR and BF in vol.
paras: Not interchangeable

the legs scale with $\sigma\sqrt{\tau}$ and move with the smile, and past second order the wings enter. The same three handles give different packages at different maturities, and RR or BF can move while the handles stay fixed.
Division of labour

persistence fills gaps: its legs sit where quotes thin out, and it ignores a level move. The filter and the graph track what every chain measures, the money, with exact handles for their covariances and for rebuilding a smile.

head: Consumer
Carries
Why this set
rows: Measured on every chain; exact, so the fit's information gives its noise; a spot move shifts it in closed form
Same carrier as the filter; the posterior is written back into an LQD smile, the node's other modes held
ATM, RR25, BF25, var swap; tail anchors at $2, 5, 10\Delta$
Acts only where unquoted; legs reach the wings; RR and BF weights sum to zero, so a level move passes through
Available; on liquid chains these legs are quoted, so the gates close

example: SPX-like smile: $\sigma_0 = 21.8\%$, $s_0 = -0.178$, $\kappa_0 = 0.024$. At $\tau = 0.75$ the $25\Delta$ legs sit at $k = +0.127$ and $-0.118$: RR25 $= -4.28$ vol points, line 3 gives $-4.34$. The same curve at one month: legs at $\pm 0.042$, RR25 $= -1.50$.
notes: Two ways to put a smile into three numbers. Different parts of the app use different ones, and the question is why.

The first line, the ATM handles. The level is the ATM vol. The skew is the slope of the vol curve in log-moneyness at the money. The curvature is its second derivative. On an LQD slice all three are exact, in closed form. The level comes from the ATM price. The skew comes from the ATM digital, the probability of finishing above the forward. The curvature comes from the density at the forward. Each is pushed through Black's formula. No finite difference of a plotted curve.

The second line, the packages. The risk reversal is the vol at the call leg minus the vol at the put leg. The butterfly is the average of the two leg vols minus the ATM vol. A 25-delta call leg is the strike where the forward Black call delta is 0.25; the put leg is where it is 0.75. The strike depends on the smile's own vol there, so it is solved by a short fixed point. The sign is call minus put by default; the Collar sign setting flips it.

The third line, the link. Expand the smile to second order at the money and read it at the legs. The risk reversal is essentially the skew times the distance between the legs. The butterfly is a quarter of the curvature times the squared legs, plus a skew term, because the legs are not symmetric in log-moneyness. To first order, the packages are the handles rescaled by the leg width.

But only to first order, for three reasons. The leg width is proportional to vol times root time, so the same handles give different packages at different maturities. The legs are solved on the smile, so they move when the smile moves. And past second order, at 10 delta especially, the wings enter. The strip: an SPX-like smile at nine months has a 25-delta risk reversal of minus 4.28 vol points; the quadratic says minus 4.34. Read the same curve at one month: the legs move in to plus or minus 0.042, and the risk reversal is minus 1.50. Same three handles, different packages. The app can even move the risk reversal or the butterfly with the three handles held fixed. So neither set is a function of the other. This is not a linear change of coordinates.

Why the ATM handles for the filter? The filter's job is a state that is observed but noisy. Every chain quotes the money densely, so the three handles are measured at every snapshot. They are exact functions of the fit, so their covariance follows from the fit's own information matrix. And they move in closed form when spot moves. The ATM vol moves by SSR times the skew times the log-forward move; the skew by the curvature times the move. A 10-delta leg has none of that. It can be unquoted, and it moves with the forward.

The graph carries the same three, as three separate fields, so the filter, the prior's baseline and the graph share one vocabulary. After the solve, each node's handles are written back into an arbitrage-free LQD smile by moving only three primary directions. The node keeps its own shape in the other modes.

Why packages for persistence? Persistence acts where today's quotes are silent. It needs coordinates whose legs reach the wings, and that do not fight a level move. The risk reversal and butterfly weights sum to zero, so an overnight jump of the whole smile passes through while yesterday's shape is kept. ATM is in the default set too, but its gate is closed whenever the money is quoted.

Could both be used everywhere? In part the app already does. The Smile factors mode persists ATM, skew and curvature, as vol differences at zero and plus or minus 0.06. On a liquid chain those legs are quoted, so the gates close and nothing is persisted. In the stored August 2024 backtest both pure modes had a median gain of zero, against 32 vol basis points for the default Hybrid. In the other direction, the filter's active prior is already written as three such rows through the same plumbing, so risk-reversal and butterfly rows could be added. That is a listed extension. The costs: a larger state; legs that move with the forward, so no closed-form transport; and 10-delta legs that are often unquoted. That last one is a gap, which is persistence's job, not the filter's.
Transition: next, SVI in its jump-wing reading. Its ATM skew handle, psi, divided by root time, is exactly the ATM skew of this slide.

If asked whether the app treats the two sets as overlapping: yes. With the filter active, the risk-reversal and butterfly persistence rows are switched off, because they would count yesterday's skew and curvature twice. Only the deep-tail rows stay.

If asked about kurtosis: the third handle in the app is curvature, the second derivative of the vol curve at the money. It reads the density at the forward, a local quantity. Kurtosis is a moment of the whole law. The curvature is its local counterpart on the smile, not the same number.

title: SVI and its Jump-Wings reading
lede: Raw SVI draws total variance as a tilted hyperbola with two straight wings; Jump-Wings reads the same curve as five desk quantities.
eq_labels: 1 · Raw SVI: a V with a rounded bottom, shifted and tilted
2 · Its wing slopes and its lowest point
3 · Jump-Wings: five readings of the same curve
eq_note: $w_0 = w(0)$. $a$ lifts the curve, $b$ scales both wings, $\rho$ tilts them, $m$ is the centre of the square root (not the minimum), $\xi$ rounds the bottom. $\sqrt{v}$: ATM vol; $\psi/\sqrt{\tau} = \sigma'(0)$, the ATM skew $s_0$; $p$, $c$: wing slopes over $\sqrt{w_0}$ (JW's names; $c$ is not a price here); $\sqrt{\tilde v}$: lowest vol.
paras: Fitting chart
raw SVI is stored; the solver moves $\beta_L, \beta_R$, the bottom $(k_*, w_*)$ and its curvature $\kappa_*$, keeping both wings below 1.95 (Lee's limit is 2) and $w_* > 0$.
Convex is not arbitrage-free
$w'' > 0$, but the density needs $w$, $w'$, $w''$ together: checked on 801 points across the quotes; a failing fit is refitted once.
alt: Reference SVI curve annotated with the ATM vol, the ATM tangent and the lowest vol, with a total-variance inset showing the two wing asymptotes
caption: Reference-note curve read in Jump-Wings: ATM vol $\sqrt{v}$, ATM tangent of slope $\psi/\sqrt{\tau}$ and lowest vol $\sqrt{\tilde v}$ on the vol chart; the wing slopes $p\sqrt{v\tau}$ and $c\sqrt{v\tau}$ only in total variance (inset).
reference: Note 02 · raw geometry, JW handles, structural chart, density certificate
notes: SVI is the market's standard one-expiry parametrisation. It draws total variance, vol squared times time, against log-moneyness.

The first line. Start from a V with a rounded bottom: the square root of the squared distance to the centre plus a rounding term, scaled by b. Then a lifts the whole curve, m slides the rounded corner sideways, rho tilts the two arms in opposite directions, and xi sets how round the bottom is. Five numbers: a, b, rho, m and xi.

The second line. Far from the money the square root is just the distance to the centre, so both wings are straight lines. The put-side slope is b times one minus rho; the call-side slope is b times one plus rho. Those are the two wing slopes on the slide. Lee's moment formula says no distribution has a total-variance wing steeper than 2. The curve bottoms out at the minimum total variance. Note that m is the centre of the square root, not the minimum: the tilt moves the minimum away from it.
Why a second language? The raw coefficients move several desk features at once. b raises both wings and the floor. Rho shifts the minimum and trades one wing against the other.

The third line, Jump-Wings. The first handle is the ATM total variance over time, so its square root is the ATM vol. The second, psi on the slide, is the slope of the square root of total variance at the money. Divided by root time, it is exactly the ATM skew of the previous slide. The next two, p and c, are the put and call wing slopes divided by the ATM total vol. Here c is Jump-Wings' own name, not a call price. The last handle is the minimum total variance over time, so its square root is the lowest vol on the curve. The figure shows where each one sits: level, tangent and floor on the vol chart; the wing slopes only in total variance, in the inset.

How the app uses it. The fit stores raw SVI. The solver works in a structural chart: the two wing slopes, the location and height of the bottom, and the curvature there. Each is mapped so that every trial point has both wings under 1.95 and a positive floor. The 1.95 is a small buffer under Lee's 2, because the boundary itself allows a negative tail density. Jump-Wings is a reading of the result; the app has no five-handle input.

Convex is not arbitrage-free. Total variance is strictly convex by construction, but the density depends on total variance, its slope and its curvature together, through Durrleman's function g. The classic counterexample passes both screens: a lowest total variance of 0.0116 and a steeper wing of 0.174. It still has g equal to minus 0.033 near a log-moneyness of 0.88, which is a negative density. So every displayed slice is checked on 801 points across the quoted strikes. A failing fit is refitted once with a penalty on negative g, and kept only if it passes.

The strip: the SPX-like smile of the previous slide is an exact SVI slice. Its Jump-Wings reading: ATM vol 21.8 percent. Skew minus 0.178, the same ATM skew as before. Wing slopes in total variance of 0.072 on the put side and 0.014 on the call side. Lowest vol 16.0 percent at a log-moneyness of 0.57, well beyond the quotes on the call side.
Transition: SVI has one minimum; it cannot turn twice. Next: MCS, which adds local bumps to a convex base without moving its wings.

If asked how well the handles are identified: take the same smile with a two-basis-point ripple, quoted from a log-moneyness of minus 0.5 to plus 0.32. An SVI fit matches the quotes to 0.43 vol bp RMS, with rho at minus 0.32 instead of minus 0.68. The ATM vol, the skew and the put wing come back. The call wing, 0.037 instead of 0.014, and the floor do not; both sit beyond the last quote. Read the handles where the quotes are.

If asked why the structural chart is the default: a benchmark run before the switch settled it. Equal or better precision in all twelve regime medians, no breaks, and about three times the speed of the raw chart.

If asked about psi equal to zero: when the ATM is the minimum, the five handles lose the curvature of the bottom. Many raw slices then share the same handles. The app's conversion from Jump-Wings to raw refuses that point.

title: MCS: a convex base plus local corrections
lede: A convex base owns the wings and the overall skew; up to two signed hats add a shoulder or a notch in the body and vanish in both wings. Not arbitrage-free by construction: the core count, a ridge, a wing penalty and the density check govern it.
eq_labels: 1 · Log-cosh: a rounded absolute value, straight far out
2 · Model: base (value, slope, curvature at $z_0$) plus $n_c \le 2$ signed hats
3 · Hat: a second difference of the same log-cosh, height 1 at $m_j$
eq_note: $\sigma_{\mathrm{ref}}$: quoted vol nearest the money; $w = \tau v$. $\gamma_-$, $\gamma_+$: how fast the left and right wings straighten; $z_0$ is fitted, so $v_0, v_1$ are not the ATM level and skew. Hat $j$: height $\alpha_j$, centre $m_j$, half-width $h_j$, sharpness $\gamma_j$.
paras: Wings untouched
a second difference of a straight line is zero, and $\Phi$ is straight far out: each hat, its slope and its curvature vanish in both wings. The wing slopes stay the base's, $v_1 \mp 2v_2/\gamma_\mp$.
alt: Reference MCS figure: a convex base, two positive hats and their W-shaped total variance
caption: Reference-note decomposition: the convex base (orange) and two hats of height $+0.019$ (dashed) add up to the W-shaped total (grey, $v_R$ in the figure); far out the total rejoins the base.
example: A hat of height $\alpha = 0.019$ on a 30% vol lifts its centre to $\sqrt{0.09 + 0.019} = 33.0\%$. Seed shape $h = 0.4$, $\gamma = 5$: 4% of it is left one unit of $z$ away, 0.03% at two.
notes: MCS, the multi-core sigmoid, answers what SVI cannot: a smile that turns twice. The W before an event, a shoulder on each side of a central trough. A convex curve has one minimum and no interior maximum, so no convex model can draw it.

Units first. MCS models the annualised implied variance, vol squared, against a normalised moneyness z. That is log-moneyness divided by a reference vol times root time, where the reference vol is the quoted vol nearest the money. So z counts standard deviations, and one unit of z means the same thing at every maturity.

The first line, the building block: the log-cosh. It is a rounded absolute value. Near zero it is a parabola, half the square of its argument; far out it is a straight line of slope two over gamma. Gamma sets how fast it straightens.

The second line, the model. The base is a value, plus a slope times the distance to the centre, plus a curvature times the log-cosh of that distance. The log-cosh and its slope vanish at zero, and its curvature there is one. So the three base coefficients are simply the base's value, slope and curvature at its centre. Two sharpness rates let the left and right wings straighten at different speeds. Six numbers. The base is convex, like SVI: it sets the wings and the overall skew. Careful: the centre is fitted, so these are not the ATM level and skew. Those are read from the full curve.
Then the corrections: up to two signed hats, each a height times a hat shape. A positive height raises a shoulder; a negative height digs a notch.

The third line, the hat. Evaluate the same log-cosh at three points: the hat's centre, and one half-width either side of it. Form the second difference: left, minus twice the middle, plus right. Divide by twice the log-cosh of the half-width, so that the height at the centre is exactly one. Four numbers per hat: height, centre, half-width, sharpness. With two cores the model has fourteen parameters.

Why the wings never move. A second difference of any straight line is zero, and the log-cosh is a straight line far out. So each hat, its slope and its curvature all vanish in both wings, and the wing slopes stay the base's. On the left that is the base slope minus twice the base curvature over the left sharpness. On the right it is the base slope plus twice the base curvature over the right sharpness. Adding cores changes the body, never the tails.
The figure: the orange base, two dashed hats of height 0.019 at plus and minus 0.2 in log-moneyness, and their grey sum, a W. Far out, the sum rejoins the base.

The strip: on a base variance of 0.09, a 30 percent vol, a hat of height 0.019 lifts the vol at its centre to 33.0 percent, three points. The height over twice the vol, 3.2, is the quick estimate. With the starting shape the fit uses, half-width 0.4 and sharpness 5, a hat keeps 4 percent of its height one unit of z from its centre. Two units away, 0.03 percent.

Flexibility is governed. MCS is not arbitrage-free by construction: a hat can bend the density negative. So the app applies several controls. At most two cores, and fewer on short chains, never more parameters than quotes. A small ridge on the heights. Hats smaller than the fit's own noise are pruned, and the fit is redone once without them. A penalty on negative g beyond the quotes, doubled on the put side. And, as for SVI, the 801-point density check with one repair refit.
Transition: that closes the smile models. Next chapter, the surface, starting with the tails and the generalised LQD tail exponents.

If asked why not three cores: in the stored backtest a third core cut the out-of-sample RMS only from 13.99 to 13.58 vol basis points. It cost about four times the fit time and more butterfly arbitrage. Two is the cap.

If asked whether the hat parameters mean anything: not one by one. Two overlapping hats can trade height, so only the curve is identified. The ATM level, skew and curvature shown for MCS are read from the full curve.
